messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo, a 51-year-old welder with a strength forged over decades of working with steel, described his life as having split into two distinct parts: before the accident, and after. It had been eight months since a drunk driver ran a red light and T-boned his pickup truck, and the robust calm he had once taken for granted had been replaced by a constant, humming vigilance. He came to therapy because his wife told him she felt like she was living with a ghost, and he couldn't find the words to tell her she was right.

The collision itself was a memory that refused to fade into the past. It lived in his body. He had been on his way home from his shop, listening to the radio, when the other car appeared from nowhere. He remembered the deafening crunch of metal, a sound that seemed to tear the world apart, followed by an unnerving silence. Before he blacked out, he was aware of three things: the sight of his dashboard crumpled against his legs, the sharp, crushing pain in his right femur and ribs, and the overwhelming stench of stale beer wafting from the other driver's shattered window. He was pinned in that position, his body contorted against the steering wheel, for what felt like an eternity before the paramedics arrived.

In the weeks that followed his physical recovery, the event began to replay itself not as a simple recollection, but as a full-body invasion. When the memory returned, it felt utterly and completely real, as if the past eight months had been a dream and he was waking up again in the wreck. He would be standing in his garage, tool in hand, and suddenly he would smell the spilled alcohol and leaking coolant, see the spiderweb of cracks on the windshield, and feel the phantom pain flare up in his leg with searing intensity. His shoulders would hunch and his right leg would lock, his muscles seizing into the exact helpless position he was in while trapped in the driver's seat. It was a complete sensory hijacking, leaving him trembling and disoriented when it finally released its grip.

Because these memories were so visceral—a reliving rather than a remembering—the elements that composed them became toxic in his present life. The memory’s power had turned the world into a minefield of its own fragments. The screech of tires on his street was no longer just a sound; it was the prelude to the impact that lived in his bones. He was at a barbecue a few months ago when a friend opened a beer, and the familiar smell sent a jolt of pure terror through him, forcing him to make an excuse and leave immediately. Driving past a fender-bender on the side of the road was unbearable; in the crumpled bumpers and broken headlights, he saw the ghost of his own mangled truck and felt the echo of the crash. The intrusive, full-sensory memory had become a lens through which he now viewed the world, sensitizing him to any sight, sound, or smell that threatened to pull him back into the wreckage.

This constant threat-monitoring has dismantled his life. At work, the sudden roar of a grinder or the loud clang of dropped sheet metal can make him flinch so badly he has to stop what he’s doing, his heart hammering against his ribs. He used to be a foreman, respected for his steady hand and calm demeanor, but he’s made several mistakes recently and feels his crew’s confidence in him waning. He no longer drives on the freeway, taking long, convoluted routes through side streets that add an hour to his commute. His marriage, once his bedrock, is strained by his new-found distance and irritability. He sits through dinner in silence, his body rigid, listening for danger. The final straw came last week when a memory was triggered while watching the evening news. An image of a car accident flashed on the screen, and the pain in his leg became so real, so immediate, that he cried out and fell to his knees. It was in that moment, seeing the fear in his wife's eyes, that he knew he couldn't live as a prisoner of his own memory any longer. He is terrified that his body will never again feel like his own, but a flicker of hope remains that he might one day be able to sit in the driver's seat and just be a man going home, not a victim returning to a crash.
